questions.question_text:
A committee of $4$ is to be chosen from a group of $10$ people.
If one specific person, Mark, must be included, how many different committees can be formed?

options.why: Calculated $^{10}C_4$, ignoring the restriction that Mark must be included.
Calculated $^{9}C_4$, excluding Mark instead of including him.
Multiplied 8 by 3 instead of evaluating the combination $^{9}C_3$.

questions.solution_text:
Fix Mark on the committee and choose $3$ from $9$ remaining:
$= {^{9}C_{3}}$
$= \dfrac{9 \times 8 \times 7}{3 \times 2 \times 1}$
$= 84$

questions.question_text:
From a club of $12$ members, a committee of $5$ is selected.
Exactly one of David and Sarah must be included and the other excluded.
How many committees are possible?

options.why: Calculated $^{12}C_{5}$, ignoring the restriction on David and Sarah.
Calculated $^{10}C_{3}$, counting committees containing both David and Sarah.
Calculated $^{10}C_{5}$, excluding both David and Sarah.

questions.solution_text:
There are $2$ choices for which of David and Sarah is included.
Choose the other $4$ members from the remaining $10$ people:
$= 2 \times {^{10}C_{4}}$
$= 2 \times 210$
$= 420$

questions.question_text:
A panel of $4$ judges is selected from $5$ lawyers and $4$ academics.
In how many ways can the panel be formed if it must contain at least $3$ lawyers?

options.why: Subtracted 10 from 45 due to an arithmetic error.
Calculated $^{9}C_4$ without enforcing the minimum requirement of 3 lawyers.

Calculated $10 \times 5 = 50$ by multiplying the two lawyer-selection counts instead of adding the mutually exclusive case counts, and omitted the $4$ choices of academic in the first case. Multiplying the actual case counts would give $40 \times 5 = 200$.

questions.solution_text:
Case 1 ($3$ lawyers, $1$ academic): $^{5}C_{3} \times {^{4}C_{1}} = 10 \times 4 = 40$
Case 2 ($4$ lawyers, $0$ academics): $^{5}C_{4} \times {^{4}C_{0}} = 5 \times 1 = 5$
Total $= 40 + 5$
$= 45$

questions.question_text:
A delegation of $3$ is chosen from $5$ men and $3$ women.
How many delegations contain more men than women?

options.why: Calculated only the case with 2 men and 1 woman, omitting the case with 3 men.
Calculated $^{8}C_3$ without considering the gender restriction.
Calculated only the case with 3 men, omitting the case with 2 men.

questions.solution_text:
More men than women in $3$ members requires $2$ men or $3$ men.
Case 1 ($2$ men, $1$ woman): $^{5}C_{2} \times {^{3}C_{1}} = 10 \times 3 = 30$
Case 2 ($3$ men, $0$ women): $^{5}C_{3} \times {^{3}C_{0}} = 10 \times 1 = 10$
Total $= 30 + 10$
$= 40$

questions.question_text:
A committee of $3$ is selected from $7$ doctors and $4$ nurses.
How many different committees contain at least one nurse?

options.why: Calculated total combinations $^{11}C_3$ without subtracting the all-doctor cases.
Calculated the number of committees with no nurses instead of at least one.
Calculated $^{4}C_{1} \times {^{7}C_{2}}$, counting exactly one nurse and omitting committees with two or three nurses.

questions.solution_text:
Total committees: $^{11}C_{3} = 165$.
All doctors (no nurses): $^{7}C_{3} = 35$.
At least one nurse $= 165 - 35$
$= 130$

questions.question_text:
$3$ letters are chosen at random without replacement from the $8$ letters in $\text{TRIANGLE}$.
In how many ways can the selection contain at least one vowel?

options.why: Calculated total combinations $^{8}C_3$ without subtracting all-consonant selections.
Counted only selections with zero vowels instead of subtracting from total.
Multiplied $^{3}C_1$ by $^{5}C_2$, failing to account for selections with multiple vowels.

questions.solution_text:
Vowels: I, A, E ($3$); Consonants: T, R, N, G, L ($5$).
Total selections: $^{8}C_{3} = 56$.
All consonants: $^{5}C_{3} = 10$.
At least one vowel $= 56 - 10$
$= 46$

questions.question_text: In how many ways can $6$ students be divided into two groups of $2$ and $4$ students respectively?

options.why: Multiplied $^{6}C_2$ by 2, incorrectly permuting the group assignments.
Calculated $^{6}C_3/2!$, dividing as if the groups had equal size.
Divided $^{6}C_{2} = 15$ by $2$, incorrectly halving an unequal partition.

questions.solution_text:
Because the group sizes are unequal ($2$ and $4$), no division by factorials is required:
$= {^{6}C_{2}} \times {^{4}C_{4}}$
$= 15 \times 1$
$= 15$

questions.question_text: In how many ways can $10$ players be divided into two teams of $5$ players each, if the two teams are unlabeled?

options.why: Calculated $^{10}C_5$ without dividing by $2!$ for the indistinguishable teams.
Multiplied 10 by 5 instead of evaluating the combination partition.
Divided by 4 instead of $2!$.

questions.solution_text:
Choose $5$ players for one team in $^{10}C_{5} = 252$ ways.
Since the two teams of $5$ are indistinguishable, divide by $2!$:
$= \dfrac{252}{2}$
$= 126$

options.why: Calculated total triples $^{9}C_3$ without subtracting the collinear points.
Subtracted $^{4}C_{2} = 6$ instead of $^{4}C_{3} = 4$ from $^{9}C_{3} = 84$.
Halved the total triangles due to confusion over vertex ordering.

questions.solution_text:
Total triples: $^{9}C_{3} = 84$.
Collinear triples: $^{4}C_{3} = 4$.
Number of triangles $= 84 - 4$
$= 80$

questions.question_text:
$11$ distinct points are arranged around a circle.
How many unordered pairs of triangles can be drawn using these points as vertices, if the two triangles have no vertices in common?

options.why: Calculated $^{11}C_{3} \times {^{8}C_{3}}$ without dividing by $2!$, counting each pair in both orders.
Calculated only $^{11}C_{6}$, omitting the $10$ ways to divide each set of six vertices into two triangles.
Calculated $^{11}C_{3}$, counting single triangles instead of pairs.

questions.solution_text:
Choose $6$ distinct vertices from the $11$ points:
$^{11}C_{6} = 462$.
Choose $3$ of these vertices for one triangle; the other $3$ form the second triangle.
Divide by $2!$ because the two triangles are indistinguishable:
$= {^{11}C_{6}} \times \dfrac{^{6}C_{3}}{2!}$
$= 462 \times \dfrac{20}{2}$
$= 4620$
